P16: Give children real agency. Kids are allowed to say no, and no grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.
P21: I also looked in the research corpus for a well-documented real case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to people, where the whole sequence is on record, from what the child did to what happened later. I didn't find one. It's possible a case like that exists and just isn't published because it's private, or because it was sent somewhere else to deal with. But it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, outside the home community's control.
P23: If the kids never leave, the community has no way of knowing whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, see other ways of living, and disagree with the founders, without treating them as traitors for it.
P25: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. Kids who grow up without ever using money especially need a decent education in how the money world operates, and what to do when they have to deal with it: jobs, rent, contracts, banks, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help. They also need skills they can take with them, people outside, their own records, and somewhere to go next. If the community can help with the move, great. If it can't, it can still avoid punishing anyone for leaving, or holding back what they need. No upbringing is perfectly free. The point is to not turn belonging into a trap.
P27: Couples who share a home, a culture and even a bed still split apart over screens, vaccination, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now imagine twenty adults with twenty different childhoods.
P28: Once a child is already living inside the disagreement, goodwill won't answer those questions, however sincere it is. There needs to be enough common ground in the principles about kids that the community is coherent, without being so rigid that people can't be parents.
H4: Talk About Child-Rearing Values Before the Kids Get Caught in the Middle
